summary: Chuichi Kimura is a Buddhist studies scholar who was attested as an associate professor in 2015 and as a former professor in 2026 at Minobusan University.

Chun-i Tang (1909–1978) was a philosopher and sinologist. He studied at Sino-Russian University, Peking University, and National Central University, where he later became a professor. He co-founded New Asia College and chaired Chinese University of Hong Kong.

Chun-min Yen is a Buddhist studies and sinology scholar who completed a PhD at the University of Arizona under doctoral supervisor Robert M. Gimello (attested 2004). Yen also studied under Todd Brown, Chanyun, and Sheng Yen.

Chögyam Trungpa (1939–1987) worked in Buddhist studies, Tibetology, and religious studies. He studied at the University of Oxford and under teachers including Khenpo Gangshar and Dilgo Khyentse Rinpoche, and founded Naropa University and Kagyu Samye Ling.
Chökyi Gyatso studied under Jamgön Kongtrul Lodrö Thayé, Thubten Chökyi Dorje, Khakyab Dorje, and Jamyang Khyentse Chökyi Lodrö, whom he also taught. He also taught Khunu Lama Tenzin Gyaltsen.
Chökyi Nyima studied under Jamyang Khyentse Chökyi Lodrö and Dudjom Rinpoche.

Chökyi Nyima Rinpoche (b. 1951) is a Buddhist studies and Tibetology scholar. He studied at Rumtek Monastery and under Rangjung Rigpe Dorje and Dilgo Khyentse Rinpoche. He founded Rangjung Yeshe Institute and became abbot of Ka-Nying Shedrub Ling.
Chönyi Drolma is a scholar of Tibetology and Buddhist studies. Attested in 2011, she studied under Thinley Norbu Rinpoche, Lama Tharchin Rinpoche, and Ngawang Zangpo.

Chün-fang Yü (b. 1938) works in Buddhist studies, religious studies, and sinology. Educated at Columbia University, she taught at Rutgers University (~1972–2001) and later served as professor and Sheng Yen Professor Emerita at Columbia.

Clara Sue Kidwell (1941–2025) was a historian who earned her PhD at the University of Oklahoma. She held posts at UC Berkeley, the National Museum of the American Indian, the University of Oklahoma, and UNC Chapel Hill.

Clare Carlisle (b. 1977) is a scholar in philosophy and religious studies. She studied at Trinity College, Cambridge (1995–2002), was a lecturer at the University of Liverpool (~2006–2011), and became a professor at King's College London (~2020).

Claude Hagège (b. 1936) is a linguist who studied at the École Normale Supérieure and under André Martinet. He held posts at the CNRS (~1965–1970), the University of Poitiers (1970–1987), and the Collège de France (1988–2006).

Claude Jacques (1929–2018) was a scholar of history, archaeology, and Indology. He studied under George Cœdès, served as director of the École française d'Extrême-Orient, and taught at the École Pratique des Hautes Études (~1970–1998).

Claude Lévi-Strauss (1908–2009) studied law and worked under Marcel Mauss. He held posts at the University of São Paulo (~1935–1939), the École Pratique des Hautes Études (~1950–1974), and the Collège de France (1959–1982).
Claudia Benthien (b. 1965) studied at Washington University in St. Louis from 1993 to 1994 and held a post at the University of Hamburg around 2005.
Claudia Weber is a scholar in Indology and religious studies who studied under Hans-Joachim Klimkeit and Gregor Ahn.

Claudius Buchanan (1766–1815) worked in Indology and religious studies. He studied at the University of Glasgow and Queens' College, Cambridge, and served as Vice-Provost of Fort William College in 1801.

Claus Oetke (1947–2019) was a scholar of Indology, philosophy, and Buddhist studies. He completed his PhD and habilitation at the University of Hamburg, and later led the Department of Indology at Stockholm University from 1993 to 2014.

Claus Vogel (1933–2012) worked in Indology and Tibetology. He completed his PhD and habilitation at the University of Marburg under Friedrich Müller and Wilhelm Rau, and was ordinarius professor at the University of Bonn from 1976 to 1998.
Clemency Montelle (b. 1977) is a scholar in Indology and history and archaeology. She held posts at the University of Canterbury in 2007 and from 2020 to 2025.
